subject: Health Education
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 1 3/4-hour practical test for 80 marks: school candidates handle and identify specimens, models, charts and first aid materials, carry out simple tests (such as food tests) and interpret health data, while private candidates take an alternative test of practical work based on drawings, photographs and data. Marks are earned for correct identification, clear labelled drawings, accurate procedures, observations and inferences, and correct calculations of health indices.

practicals.title: Food tests for starch and reducing sugars
practicals.aim: To test common Nigerian foods for the presence of starch (iodine test) and reducing sugars (Benedict's or Fehling's test) and relate the results to their nutrient class.
apparatus: Bunsen burner, spirit lamp or hot plate
materials: Food samples: yam, garri, rice, ripe banana, orange juice, glucose powder, table sugar
safety: Wear eye protection and use a test-tube holder when heating
Heat in a water bath, never point the tube at anyone
Iodine stains skin and clothes; wipe spills at once
Do not taste any laboratory sample
procedure: Grind a small piece of each solid food with about 5 cm3 of water and filter or allow to settle; use the liquid as the food solution.
Starch test: place a little of each solid sample (or 2 cm3 of solution) on a white tile or in a test tube and add 2-3 drops of iodine solution.
Record the colour: blue-black means starch present; yellow-brown (unchanged iodine) means starch absent.
Reducing sugar test: put 2 cm3 of each food solution in a clean test tube and add an equal volume (2 cm3) of Benedict's solution.
Heat the tubes in a boiling water bath for about 5 minutes.
Observe the colour change: blue (none) through green, yellow, orange to brick-red (much reducing sugar).
Repeat with table sugar (sucrose); it stays blue unless first boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid and neutralised.
Record all results in a table of test, observation and inference.
practicals.expectedObservations: Yam, garri and rice turn blue-black with iodine. Glucose, ripe banana and orange juice give green to brick-red precipitates with Benedict's solution. Table sugar remains blue with Benedict's solution because sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Results table example (7 samples): starch positive - yam, garri, rice = 3 of 7 = 42.9%; reducing sugar positive - glucose, ripe banana, orange juice = 3 of 7 = 42.9%; table sugar negative for both. Volumes: 2 cm3 food solution + 2 cm3 Benedict's = 4 cm3 in each tube, so for 7 tubes you need 7 x 2 = 14 cm3 of Benedict's solution.
precautions: Use clean test tubes for each sample to avoid contamination
Use equal volumes of food solution and reagent
Heat in a water bath, not directly in a flame
sourcesOfError: Dirty test tubes carrying sugar from one sample to another
Heating for too short a time
Very dilute food solutions giving faint colours
commonMistakes: Writing "starch is present" without stating the colour observed
Expecting table sugar to give a brick-red colour
examTips: Use a three-column table: Test, Observation, Inference
Quote exact colours (blue-black, brick-red) - vague words lose marks
Name the reagent and state the need for heating

checkQuestions.q: Which colour shows starch is present in the iodine test?
Which sample gives a negative Benedict's test without acid hydrolysis?
Why is the Benedict's test carried out in a water bath?
options: The reaction needs heat and the bath heats safely and evenly
checkQuestions.explanation: Heat is required; a water bath avoids spitting and cracking.

practicals.title: Food tests for protein and fats/oils
practicals.aim: To test foods for protein (Biuret test) and for fats and oils (grease-spot and Sudan III tests).
materials: Egg white, beans, groundnut, palm oil, milk, garri
safety: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive: wear goggles and wash spills off skin with plenty of water
Keep Sudan III (in alcohol) away from flames
Do not taste samples
procedure: Prepare food solutions or suspensions by grinding each sample with water.
Biuret test: to 2 cm3 of food solution add 2 cm3 of dilute sodium hydroxide and shake.
Add 1% copper(II) sulphate solution drop by drop, shaking after each drop.
Record the colour: violet/purple means protein present; blue (unchanged) means absent.
Grease-spot test: rub a small piece of groundnut or a drop of palm oil on paper, leave to dry for 10 minutes and hold the paper up to the light.
A translucent spot that does not disappear on drying shows fat or oil; a water spot dries off.
Sudan III test (optional): shake the sample with water and 3 drops of Sudan III; a red-stained oily layer floating on top shows fat.
Record results in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Egg white, beans and milk give a violet colour with the Biuret test. Groundnut, palm oil and milk leave a permanent translucent spot and a red layer with Sudan III. Garri gives negative results for both.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Energy link: 10 g of groundnut contains roughly 5 g fat, 2.5 g protein and 1.5 g carbohydrate, giving 5 x 9 + 2.5 x 4 + 1.5 x 4 = 45 + 10 + 6 = 61 kcal. Fat supplies 45 / 61 x 100 = 73.8% of the energy, explaining why groundnut gives a strong grease-spot result.
precautions: Add copper(II) sulphate drop by drop
Let the paper dry before judging the grease spot
Use clean apparatus for each food
sourcesOfError: Excess copper(II) sulphate masking the violet colour with blue
Water spots mistaken for grease spots if not dried
commonMistakes: Adding copper(II) sulphate before sodium hydroxide
Judging the grease spot while still wet
examTips: State "violet/purple" for protein - not "pink" or "blue"
Explain why the paper is dried in the grease-spot test

checkQuestions.q: A positive Biuret test gives
checkQuestions.explanation: Peptide bonds react with alkaline copper(II) to give violet.

checkQuestions.q: In the grease-spot test the paper is left to dry so that
checkQuestions.explanation: Only fat leaves a permanent translucent spot.

checkQuestions.q: How many kilocalories does 1 g of fat supply?
checkQuestions.explanation: Fat yields about 9 kcal per gram.

practicals.title: Planning a balanced meal and calculating its energy value
practicals.aim: To plan a balanced meal from local foods, classify its foods into nutrient classes and calculate its energy value.
materials: Sample foods or pictures: rice, beans, fish, vegetables (ugu/spinach), palm oil, orange
safety: Wash hands before handling food samples
procedure: Choose a meal for a named person (e.g. an SS3 student) containing all six classes of food.
List each food with its main nutrient class (carbohydrate, protein, fat/oil, vitamins, mineral salts, water).
Weigh or estimate the portion of each food.
Use a food composition table to find grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat in each portion.
Calculate the energy using 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat.
Compare the total with the person's needs and suggest adjustments.
practicals.expectedObservations: The meal includes an energy food, a body-building food, a protective food (vegetables/fruit) and water; most energy comes from carbohydrate.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Meal of jollof rice, beans, fish and vegetable: 75 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein, 15 g fat. Energy = 75 x 4 + 20 x 4 + 15 x 9 = 300 + 80 + 135 = 515 kcal. Share from carbohydrate = 300 / 515 x 100 = 58.3%; from fat = 135 / 515 x 100 = 26.2%; from protein = 15.5%. If a student needs about 2,400 kcal a day, this meal supplies 515 / 2400 x 100 = 21.5%.
precautions: Use the correct energy factor for each nutrient
Weigh foods raw or cooked consistently with the table used
sourcesOfError: Composition tables differ from local varieties
commonMistakes: Omitting water and fruits/vegetables from the meal
examTips: Show each multiplication step and units (kcal)
Name a local example for each food class

checkQuestions.q: What is the energy from 20 g of protein?
Which food in jollof rice, beans and fish is mainly body-building?
A meal providing 75 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 15 g fat supplies

practicals.title: Vision screening with the Snellen chart
practicals.aim: To screen the visual acuity of each eye using a Snellen chart and record results as Snellen fractions.
apparatus: Snellen chart (or E-chart for those who cannot read letters)
materials: Masking tape to mark the 6 m line
safety: Do not press on the eye being covered
Clean the occluder between students
Refer, do not diagnose - any defect goes to an eye specialist
procedure: Hang the chart at eye level in a well-lit place, avoiding glare from windows.
Measure 6 metres from the chart and mark the standing line.
Let the student stand at the line (with glasses on if usually worn) and cover the left eye with the occluder.
Point to letters from the top line downwards; the student reads each one aloud.
Record the smallest line on which the student reads most letters correctly (e.g. at least 4 of 5).
Repeat for the left eye, then both eyes.
Record each result as a fraction: testing distance / line number (e.g. 6/12).
Refer anyone with 6/12 or worse in either eye, or who squints or strains, to an optometrist or ophthalmologist.
practicals.expectedObservations: A normal eye reads the 6 m line (6/6). A short-sighted (myopic) student reads only the larger lines, e.g. 6/18; some students may show a difference between the two eyes.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A result of 6/18 means the student reads at 6 m what a normal eye reads at 18 m. Decimal acuity = 6 / 18 = 0.33 (normal = 6/6 = 1.0). In a class of 40 screened, 6 students scored 6/12 or worse: referral rate = 6 / 40 x 100 = 15%.
precautions: Prevent the student from memorising the chart
examTips: Explain the meaning of the numerator (testing distance) and the denominator
Link results to defects: myopia - difficulty with distant objects, corrected with concave lenses

checkQuestions.q: At what distance is the standard Snellen test usually done?
checkQuestions.explanation: The standard testing distance is 6 metres (20 feet).

checkQuestions.q: A result of 6/24 means the student
options: reads at 6 m what a normal eye reads at 24 m
reads at 24 m what others read at 6 m
checkQuestions.explanation: The denominator is the distance a normal eye could read that line.

checkQuestions.q: If 8 of 50 students are referred, the referral rate is

practicals.title: Simple auditory screening (watch-tick and tuning-fork tests)
practicals.aim: To screen hearing using a ticking watch and a tuning fork (Rinne and Weber tests) and distinguish possible conductive from sensorineural impairment.
safety: Never strike the tuning fork on a hard surface or near the ear; strike on the knee or rubber pad
Do not insert anything into the ear canal
procedure: Work in a quiet room. Ask the student to close the eyes and cover one ear.
Watch-tick test: bring the watch slowly towards the uncovered ear and measure the distance at which the tick is first heard; repeat for the other ear.
Rinne test: strike the fork, place its base on the mastoid bone behind the ear and time how long the sound is heard (bone conduction).
When the sound fades, move the prongs 2-3 cm from the ear canal and time how long it is still heard (air conduction).
Weber test: place the base of the vibrating fork on the middle of the forehead and ask in which ear the sound is louder.
Record results and refer abnormal findings to an ENT doctor or audiologist (audiometry).
practicals.expectedObservations: Normal: air conduction lasts about twice as long as bone conduction (Rinne positive) and the Weber sound is central. In conductive loss (e.g. wax, otitis media) bone conduction is longer and the Weber sound goes to the affected ear; in sensorineural loss Weber goes to the better ear.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rinne example: bone conduction heard for 15 s, then air conduction for a further 15 s, so total air conduction = 30 s. AC : BC = 30 : 15 = 2 : 1, normal (Rinne positive). If BC = 25 s and AC = 10 s, AC < BC - suggests conductive loss. Watch test: right ear 90 cm, left ear 30 cm; the left ear hears at only 30 / 90 = one third of the distance and should be referred.
precautions: Keep the fork prongs from touching the ear or hair
sourcesOfError: Striking the fork with different strength
commonMistakes: Confusing which test is Rinne and which is Weber
examTips: State the frequency of the fork (512 Hz) and where it is placed
Name the specialist (otologist/ENT, audiologist)

checkQuestions.q: In a normal Rinne test
options: bone conduction is longer than air conduction
air conduction is longer than bone conduction

checkQuestions.q: The tuning fork usually used in screening is
checkQuestions.explanation: 512 Hz is standard for Rinne and Weber tests.

checkQuestions.q: Wax blocking the ear canal causes
checkQuestions.explanation: Wax blocks the conduction of sound.

practicals.title: Posture assessment and identification of postural defects
practicals.aim: To assess standing, sitting and lifting posture using a plumb line and simple observations, and identify signs of kyphosis, lordosis, scoliosis and flat foot.
materials: Water and a tray or paper for footprints
safety: Lift only light loads; bend the knees, keep the back straight
Respect privacy: assess over PE kit, same-sex pairs where appropriate
procedure: Side view: hang the plumb line beside the standing student; in good posture it passes through the ear lobe, shoulder, hip, slightly behind the knee and in front of the ankle.
Back view: check that shoulders and hips are level; measure the height of each shoulder from the floor.
Ask the student to bend forward; a rib hump on one side suggests scoliosis.
Footprint test: wet the feet and stand on paper; a full sole print with no inner arch suggests flat foot.
Observe sitting posture at a desk and correct lifting technique with the box.
Record findings on the checklist and suggest corrective exercises or referral to a physiotherapist.
practicals.expectedObservations: Good posture shows a vertical alignment and level shoulders. Kyphosis shows rounded upper back; lordosis an exaggerated lower-back curve; scoliosis a sideways curve with uneven shoulders; flat foot a full footprint.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Shoulder height: right 142 cm, left 140 cm, difference = 2 cm, which may indicate scoliosis and needs referral. Class results: 9 of 36 students showed rounded shoulders = 9 / 36 x 100 = 25%.
precautions: Students should stand relaxed in their usual posture
sourcesOfError: Students correcting posture because they are observed
commonMistakes: Not linking defects to their causes (bad sitting, heavy bags)
examTips: Draw and label the plumb-line points
For each defect state a cause and a correction

checkQuestions.q: An exaggerated inward curve of the lower back is
A sideways curvature of the spine is
If 9 of 36 students have a defect, the percentage is

practicals.title: Measuring pulse rate at rest and after exercise
practicals.aim: To measure the radial pulse at rest and after exercise and show how heart rate changes and recovers.
apparatus: Stopwatch or watch with seconds hand
safety: Students with asthma, sickle cell disease or heart conditions should not do vigorous exercise
Stop if dizzy or breathless
procedure: Sit quietly for 5 minutes.
Find the radial pulse on the thumb side of the wrist using two fingers (not the thumb).
Count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute; repeat twice and average.
Do 2 minutes of step-ups or skipping.
Immediately measure the pulse again for 15 seconds.
Measure every minute for 5 minutes while resting.
Plot pulse rate (y-axis) against time (x-axis).
practicals.expectedObservations: The pulse rises sharply after exercise and falls back towards the resting value within a few minutes; fitter students recover faster.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rest: 18 beats in 15 s = 18 x 4 = 72 beats/min. After exercise: 33 beats in 15 s = 132 beats/min. Increase = 132 - 72 = 60 beats/min = 60 / 72 x 100 = 83.3% rise. After 3 minutes: 20 beats in 15 s = 80 beats/min, only 8 above rest.
precautions: Use fingers not the thumb (the thumb has its own pulse)
sourcesOfError: Pulse missed when pressing too hard
commonMistakes: Joining graph points carelessly or not labelling axes
examTips: Show the multiplication from the count to beats per minute
Explain the rise: muscles need more oxygen and glucose

checkQuestions.q: 21 beats counted in 15 seconds give a pulse rate of
Why should the thumb not be used to feel the pulse?
checkQuestions.explanation: You may count your own pulse.

checkQuestions.q: Heart rate rises during exercise mainly because
checkQuestions.explanation: More blood delivers oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.

practicals.title: Measuring height and weight and calculating Body Mass Index
practicals.aim: To measure height and weight accurately and calculate Body Mass Index (BMI) as an indicator of nutritional status.
apparatus: Stadiometer or measuring tape fixed to a wall
safety: Respect privacy and sensitivity about weight; results are confidential
Ensure the scale is on a firm level floor
procedure: Check the scale reads zero; weigh the student without shoes and in light clothing; record to 0.1 kg.
Measure height without shoes, heels together against the wall, looking straight ahead; lower a set square onto the head; record to 0.1 cm.
Convert height to metres.
Calculate BMI = weight (kg) / height (m) squared.
Classify the result (adults: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 normal, 25-29.9 overweight, 30 and above obese; for teenagers use BMI-for-age charts).
Discuss diet and exercise advice for each category.
practicals.expectedObservations: Most students fall in the normal range; some may be underweight or overweight, showing the need for balanced diet and exercise.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Student A: 60 kg, 1.65 m. BMI = 60 / (1.65 x 1.65) = 60 / 2.7225 = 22.0 kg/m2 (normal). Student B: 45 kg, 1.52 m: BMI = 45 / 2.3104 = 19.5 (normal). Adult C: 78 kg, 1.70 m: BMI = 78 / 2.89 = 27.0 (overweight).
sourcesOfError: Head not level when measuring height
commonMistakes: Using height in centimetres in the formula
examTips: Write the formula and units kg/m2
Round sensibly (1 decimal place)

For an adult, a BMI of 27 is classified as
In the BMI formula height must be in

practicals.title: Identifying types of teeth and simple dental inspection
practicals.aim: To identify incisors, canines, premolars and molars on a skull, jaw model or chart, draw a tooth in section and inspect the mouth for signs of caries and gingivitis.
apparatus: Human or animal jaw/skull or dental model
materials: Wall chart of a tooth in longitudinal section
safety: Wear gloves when handling specimens and wash hands afterwards
Use your own mirror; never share toothbrushes
procedure: Examine the model and identify each type of tooth by shape: chisel-shaped incisors, pointed canines, two-cusped premolars and broad multi-cusped molars.
Count the teeth in one half of each jaw and write the dental formula.
Draw and label a longitudinal section of a molar: enamel, dentine, pulp cavity, gum, cement, root, blood vessels and nerves.
With a mirror and torch, look at your own teeth and gums for black spots/holes (caries), bleeding or swollen gums (gingivitis) and plaque.
Demonstrate correct brushing for 2 minutes twice daily.
Record findings and advice.
practicals.expectedObservations: An adult has 32 permanent teeth; children have 20 milk teeth. Signs of caries are dark cavities; gingivitis shows red, swollen, bleeding gums.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Adult dental formula (one side, upper/lower): incisors 2/2, canine 1/1, premolars 2/2, molars 3/3 = 8 teeth per half-jaw; total = (2 + 1 + 2 + 3) x 2 x 2 = 32. Milk teeth: (2 + 1 + 2) x 2 x 2 = 20. Survey: 14 of 40 students with visible caries = 35%.
sourcesOfError: Missing or damaged teeth in specimens
examTips: Draw large, clear outlines with labels on the right
State a function for each tooth type

checkQuestions.q: How many permanent teeth does an adult human normally have?
The hardest substance in the body is
checkQuestions.explanation: Enamel covers the crown and is the hardest tissue.

checkQuestions.q: Bleeding, swollen gums suggest
checkQuestions.explanation: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums.

practicals.title: Study of the skeleton, bones and joints
practicals.aim: To identify the main bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton and the types of joints on a skeleton model or chart.
apparatus: Mammalian bones (e.g. cow femur, goat vertebrae from the market)
safety: Wear gloves when handling real bones; wash hands afterwards
Handle models carefully
procedure: Divide the skeleton into axial (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and appendicular (limbs, girdles) parts.
Identify named bones: cranium, mandible, clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, pelvis, femur, tibia, fibula.
Identify the regions of the vertebral column: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal.
Locate examples of joints: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (wrist bones), fixed (skull sutures).
Draw and label a synovial joint: bone, cartilage, synovial membrane, synovial fluid, capsule, ligament.
Demonstrate the movement allowed at each joint on your own body.
practicals.expectedObservations: The adult skeleton has 206 bones; ball-and-socket joints allow movement in all planes, hinge joints in one plane, and sutures allow no movement.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Adult skeleton: 206 bones = 80 axial + 126 appendicular. Axial share = 80 / 206 x 100 = 38.8%. Vertebral column: 7 cervical + 12 thoracic + 5 lumbar = 24 movable vertebrae, plus the fused sacrum and coccyx.
precautions: Use correct orientation when identifying left and right bones
commonMistakes: Confusing tendons (muscle to bone) with ligaments (bone to bone)
examTips: State the type of joint and the movement it allows
Give the function of synovial fluid (lubrication, reduces friction)

checkQuestions.q: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
The knee is an example of a
checkQuestions.explanation: It moves mainly in one plane.

checkQuestions.q: Which structure joins bone to bone?

practicals.title: Study of mammalian reproductive organs and pregnancy dating
practicals.aim: To identify the parts of the male and female reproductive systems on models, charts or a dissected small mammal and calculate ovulation and expected delivery dates.
apparatus: Models or charts of human reproductive systems
Dissected rat or rabbit (teacher demonstration, preserved)
safety: Specimens are preserved in chemicals; wear gloves and do not touch the face
Teacher alone handles scalpels
Treat the topic maturely and respectfully
procedure: Identify on the female model: ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus, cervix, vagina; state the function of each.
Identify on the male model: testes, scrotum, epididymis, sperm duct, seminal vesicle, prostate gland, urethra, penis.
Observe the teacher's dissected mammal and compare its organs with the human models.
Draw and label either system.
Use a calendar to work out the likely ovulation day and the expected date of delivery from given dates.
practicals.expectedObservations: The specimen shows paired gonads and ducts similar to the human pattern; the rat and rabbit have two separate uterine horns (a duplex uterus) that hold several embryos, unlike the single pear-shaped human uterus.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period: in a 28-day cycle on day 28 - 14 = 14; in a 32-day cycle on day 32 - 14 = 18. Expected delivery date (Naegele's rule): first day of last period 10 January 2026 + 1 year - 3 months + 7 days = 17 October 2026, which equals 280 days (40 weeks) after 10 January 2026.
precautions: Do not damage organs when moving them
sourcesOfError: Shrinkage and colour change in preserved specimens
Irregular cycles making ovulation estimates unreliable
commonMistakes: Confusing the oviduct and the ureter
examTips: Give the function with each labelled part
Show date calculations step by step

checkQuestions.q: Fertilisation normally takes place in the
checkQuestions.explanation: The egg meets sperm in the oviduct (fallopian tube).

checkQuestions.q: In a 30-day cycle, ovulation is likely on day
Normal human gestation is about
checkQuestions.explanation: 40 weeks = 280 days from the last period.

practicals.title: First aid for cuts, bleeding, burns and scalds
practicals.aim: To identify first aid kit items and demonstrate correct first aid for cuts, severe bleeding, burns and scalds.
apparatus: First aid box: sterile dressings, crepe and triangular bandages, gauze, adhesive plasters, cotton wool, scissors, safety pins, gloves, antiseptic, cling film
safety: Wear disposable gloves to avoid contact with blood
Never burst blisters or apply oil, toothpaste or raw egg to burns
Call for help (e.g. 112 in Nigeria) for serious injuries
procedure: Identify each item in the first aid box and state its use.
Minor cut: wash hands, put on gloves, rinse the wound under clean running water, pat dry and cover with a sterile plaster or dressing.
Severe bleeding: apply firm direct pressure with a pad, raise the injured part above the heart if no fracture, and bandage the pad firmly; add another pad if blood soaks through.
Keep the casualty lying down and watch for shock (pale, cold, clammy skin, fast weak pulse).
Burn or scald: cool under cool running water for at least 20 minutes; remove rings or tight items before swelling.
Cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing and seek medical help for large, deep or facial burns.
practicals.expectedObservations: Firm pressure and elevation slow bleeding; cooled burns become less painful and damage is reduced.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Timing: maintain direct pressure for at least 10 minutes; cool a burn for at least 20 minutes - from 13:05 cooling should continue until 13:25. A survey of a class first aid box listing 15 standard items found 9 present: 9 / 15 x 100 = 60% complete, so 6 items need replacing.
precautions: Do not remove objects embedded in a wound - pad around them
sourcesOfError: Role play may not reflect real stress
commonMistakes: Using ice or butter on burns
Removing clothing stuck to a burn
examTips: State the aims of first aid: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery
Give steps in correct order with reasons

checkQuestions.q: For how long should a burn be cooled with running water?
checkQuestions.explanation: At least 20 minutes of cool running water is advised.

checkQuestions.q: The first action for severe bleeding is
Which should NOT be put on a burn?
checkQuestions.explanation: Oils retain heat and increase infection risk.

practicals.title: First aid for fractures and dislocations: slings and splints
practicals.aim: To recognise signs of fractures and dislocations and immobilise injured limbs with slings and improvised splints.
apparatus: Splints (flat wood, rolled newspaper or cardboard)
safety: Do not try to straighten a deformed limb or push back a dislocated joint
Do not move a casualty with suspected spinal injury unless in danger
procedure: Recognise signs: pain, swelling, deformity, loss of function, abnormal movement, grating.
Keep the casualty still and support the injured part in the position found.
Arm or collarbone injury: support the forearm across the chest with an arm sling tied at the hollow above the collarbone on the uninjured side.
Leg injury: pad between the legs and tie the injured leg to the good leg (or to a padded splint) above and below the injury, knots on the uninjured side.
Check circulation beyond the bandage (colour, warmth, capillary refill) every 10 minutes and loosen if needed.
Arrange transport to hospital and treat for shock.
practicals.expectedObservations: The limb is immobilised comfortably, circulation remains normal and pain from movement is reduced.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Capillary refill: press the nail bed for 5 seconds; colour should return within 2 seconds. If it takes 4 seconds after bandaging, the bandage is too tight - loosen it. For a lower-leg fracture use at least 4 ties: 2 above and 2 below the fracture (including the ankle and knee).
precautions: Tie knots away from the injury
sourcesOfError: Role play cannot reproduce real swelling or pain
commonMistakes: Tying bandages over the fracture site
examTips: Distinguish open (compound) from closed (simple) fractures
Mention checking circulation

checkQuestions.q: A fracture where the bone breaks through the skin is
checkQuestions.explanation: An open fracture has a wound connecting to the bone.

checkQuestions.q: Colour returning to a pressed nail bed should take no more than about
checkQuestions.explanation: Delay over 2 s suggests poor circulation.

checkQuestions.q: A dislocated shoulder should be
options: pushed back by the first aider
supported and the casualty taken to hospital
checkQuestions.explanation: Only trained medical staff reduce dislocations.

practicals.title: Asphyxia: recovery position and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
practicals.aim: To demonstrate the recovery position and adult CPR on a manikin, and first aid for choking and suffocation.
apparatus: CPR manikin (or firm pillow for rhythm practice)
Stopwatch or metronome app set to 110 bpm
safety: Practise compressions only on a manikin, never on a person
Check for danger before approaching a casualty (traffic, electricity, smoke)
procedure: Use DRABC: check Danger, Response (shout and tap shoulders), shout for help, open the Airway (head tilt, chin lift), check Breathing for up to 10 seconds.
If breathing normally, place the casualty in the recovery position (on the side, top leg bent, head tilted back) and monitor.
If not breathing normally, call 112 and start CPR: hands in the centre of the chest, arms straight.
Give 30 compressions at 100-120 per minute, 5-6 cm deep, allowing full recoil.
Give 2 rescue breaths (seal the mouth, pinch the nose, watch the chest rise), or continue compressions only if unwilling or untrained.
Continue 30:2 until help arrives or the person recovers; choking adults: up to 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts.
practicals.expectedObservations: Correct hand position and rhythm cause the manikin chest to compress and recoil fully; the recovery position keeps the airway open and allows fluids to drain.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Compression rate: 30 compressions at 110 per minute take 30 / 110 x 60 = 16.4 seconds. Five cycles of 30:2 = 150 compressions and 10 breaths; at 110/min compressions alone take 150 / 110 = 1.36 minutes (about 82 s), plus roughly 5 x 5 s for breaths = about 107 s, close to 2 minutes, which is when rescuers should swap.
precautions: Keep interruptions to compressions under 10 seconds
sourcesOfError: Manikins differ from real chest resistance
commonMistakes: Compressing too shallowly or too fast
examTips: Quote the ratio 30:2 and the rate 100-120 per minute
Mention calling for help early

checkQuestions.q: The compression-to-breath ratio for adult CPR is
checkQuestions.explanation: Current guidance is 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

checkQuestions.q: The recommended compression rate is
An unconscious casualty who is breathing normally should be
checkQuestions.explanation: The recovery position keeps the airway open.

practicals.title: Preparing oral rehydration solution (ORS)
practicals.aim: To prepare oral rehydration solution from a WHO/UNICEF sachet and by the home salt-sugar method, and explain its use in diarrhoea.
apparatus: 1-litre measuring jug or clean 1-litre bottle (e.g. empty water bottle)
safety: Wash hands with soap before preparing
Use exactly the stated amount of water; too little water makes the solution too salty
Discard ORS after 24 hours
procedure: Boil water and allow it to cool.
Sachet method: pour the whole sachet into exactly 1 litre of cooled boiled water and stir until dissolved.
Home method: measure 1 litre of cooled boiled water; add 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt; stir well.
Taste: it should be no saltier than tears.
Give in small, frequent sips with a cup and spoon; continue breastfeeding and normal feeding.
Give zinc tablets as advised by a health worker and seek care if the child shows danger signs (blood in stool, sunken eyes, inability to drink, lethargy).
practicals.expectedObservations: A clear, slightly sweet and slightly salty solution; with ORS the dehydrated child gradually passes urine and becomes more alert.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Home recipe for 1 litre: 6 level teaspoons sugar (about 6 x 5 ml = 30 ml) and 1/2 level teaspoon salt (about 2.5 ml). For 500 ml halve it: 3 teaspoons sugar and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Fluid guide: after each loose stool a child under 2 years gets 50-100 ml; a child who passes 6 loose stools in a day at 100 ml each needs 600 ml extra.
sourcesOfError: Using a container that is not exactly 1 litre
commonMistakes: Dissolving a sachet in less water
Giving soft drinks instead of ORS
examTips: Quote the exact proportions and the volume of water
State that ORS replaces water and salts lost and prevents dehydration

checkQuestions.explanation: WHO home recipe: 6 level teaspoons sugar, half a level teaspoon salt.

practicals.title: Simple household water purification
practicals.aim: To purify muddy water by sedimentation, filtration and boiling and compare the clarity of water from different sources.
materials: Samples from a stream, well, borehole and rain
safety: Never drink unboiled test samples
Take care with boiling water and stoves
Wash hands after handling stream water
procedure: Collect equal volumes (500 ml) of water from different sources and note colour, smell and particles.
Sedimentation: leave samples to stand for 1 hour (or add a pinch of alum and stir) and observe settling.
Decant the top water carefully into the filter made of layers: gravel at the bottom, sand, charcoal and cloth at top (or as constructed), and collect the filtrate.
Boil the filtered water at a rolling boil for at least 1 minute, cover and allow to cool.
Store in a clean covered container and draw with a clean cup.
Compare clarity before and after each stage.
practicals.expectedObservations: Mud settles at the bottom; filtered water is clearer; boiling kills most germs though it does not remove dissolved chemicals. Borehole and rainwater are usually clearer than stream water.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Household needs: a family of 6 using 20 litres per person per day needs 6 x 20 = 120 litres daily and 120 x 30 = 3,600 litres in 30 days. Filtration rate example: 500 ml collected in 4 minutes = 125 ml per minute, so 10 litres would take 10,000 / 125 = 80 minutes.
precautions: Do not stir the sediment when decanting
commonMistakes: Believing clear water is always safe
Storing treated water in uncovered buckets
examTips: List purification stages in order with the purpose of each
Name water-borne diseases prevented (cholera, typhoid, dysentery)

checkQuestions.q: Which method kills most disease germs in water at home?
checkQuestions.explanation: Boiling kills bacteria, viruses and parasites.

practicals.title: Household and school waste disposal survey
practicals.aim: To survey methods of refuse and sewage disposal used by households near the school and assess their health hazards.
safety: Work in groups with a teacher; do not enter dumpsites or open drains
Wear gloves and masks; wash hands after the survey
procedure: Prepare a short questionnaire on refuse disposal (bin collection/PSP, open dumping, burning, burying, composting) and toilet type.
Visit a sample of households (e.g. 40) with permission and record answers.
Observe drains, dumpsites and pests (flies, rats, mosquitoes) and take photographs.
Tally the results and calculate percentages.
Draw a bar chart or pie chart of disposal methods.
Write a short report with recommendations to the community or local government.
practicals.expectedObservations: Common methods include open dumping and burning; blocked drains and refuse heaps attract flies, rats and mosquitoes and cause odour and flooding.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Survey of 40 households: open dumping 28 (28 / 40 x 100 = 70%), collection by waste vendor 6 (15%), burning 4 (10%), burying 2 (5%); total 40 = 100%. Pie chart angles: 70% x 360 = 252 degrees, 15% = 54, 10% = 36, 5% = 18 (sum 360).
precautions: Ask permission and keep answers confidential
Use a fair sample of streets
examTips: State a health hazard and a remedy for each method
Show percentage and angle calculations

practicals.title: Mosquito breeding site survey and vector control
practicals.aim: To locate mosquito breeding sites around homes and the school, calculate larval indices and recommend control measures.
materials: Charts of vectors: Anopheles, Aedes, Culex, housefly, cockroach, rat, tsetse fly
safety: Wear gloves and long sleeves; avoid stagnant drains and deep water
Do not handle rats or dead animals
procedure: Identify vectors from charts and the diseases they spread (Anopheles - malaria; Aedes - yellow fever, dengue; Culex - filariasis; housefly - cholera, typhoid; tsetse - sleeping sickness).
Inspect compounds for water-holding containers: tyres, tins, flower pots, water drums, gutters, blocked drains.
Dip water from each container and look for larvae and pupae; record positive containers and houses.
Use a hand lens to tell Anopheles larvae (lie parallel to the water surface) from Culex/Aedes larvae (hang at an angle with a siphon).
Calculate the larval indices.
Recommend and, where possible, carry out control: emptying and covering containers, clearing drains, insecticide-treated nets, indoor spraying.
practicals.expectedObservations: Larvae are often found in discarded tyres, tins and uncovered water drums; Anopheles larvae lie flat at the surface; Culex larvae are common in dirty drains.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Survey of 60 houses: 12 houses had larvae; 45 containers inspected, 9 positive; 18 positive containers counted across all 60 houses. House index = 12 / 60 x 100 = 20%. Container index = 9 / 45 x 100 = 20%. Breteau index = 18 positive containers per 60 houses x 100 = 30 per 100 houses.
commonMistakes: Listing only insecticide spraying as control
examTips: Distinguish physical, chemical and biological control with examples
Link each vector to its disease and pathogen

checkQuestions.explanation: Anopheles larvae lack a siphon and lie flat.

practicals.title: Calculating and interpreting vital statistics
practicals.aim: To calculate crude birth rate, crude death rate, infant mortality rate, rate of natural increase and morbidity rates from given community data.
materials: Local health records or given data set (e.g. from a primary health centre)
safety: Keep personal health records confidential; use anonymised data
procedure: Collect or read the data: mid-year population, live births, deaths, infant deaths and new cases of a disease in one year.
Crude birth rate = live births / population x 1,000.
Crude death rate = deaths / population x 1,000.
Infant mortality rate = deaths under 1 year / live births x 1,000.
Rate of natural increase (%) = (births - deaths) / population x 100.
Incidence of a disease = new cases / population at risk x 1,000; draw a bar chart and interpret the results.
practicals.expectedObservations: The figures show whether the population is growing and highlight health problems such as high infant mortality, guiding health planning.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Community of 50,000: 1,250 live births, 400 deaths, 30 infant deaths, 600 new malaria cases. CBR = 1,250 / 50,000 x 1,000 = 25 per 1,000. CDR = 400 / 50,000 x 1,000 = 8 per 1,000. IMR = 30 / 1,250 x 1,000 = 24 per 1,000 live births. Natural increase = (1,250 - 400) / 50,000 x 100 = 1.7%. Malaria incidence = 600 / 50,000 x 1,000 = 12 per 1,000.
precautions: Use the correct denominator (live births for IMR)
commonMistakes: Dividing infant deaths by the total population
examTips: Write each formula before substituting
State one use of each statistic (planning, evaluating programmes)

Infant mortality rate uses which denominator?
checkQuestions.explanation: IMR = infant deaths per 1,000 live births.

practicals.title: Study of parasitic worms and their life cycles
practicals.aim: To identify preserved specimens or charts of roundworm, tapeworm, hookworm and guinea worm and describe their life cycles and prevention.
apparatus: Preserved specimens in labelled jars (if available)
safety: Do not open specimen jars; preservatives are toxic
Wash hands after the practical
procedure: Observe each specimen or chart and note shape, size, segmentation and special features (tapeworm scolex with hooks and suckers, hookworm mouth hooks).
Trace the life cycle on the chart: source of infection, entry route, site in the body, how eggs or larvae leave the host.
Draw and label one worm and its life cycle as a flow diagram.
Relate each stage to a preventive measure (e.g. wearing shoes prevents hookworm larvae entering through the skin).
Summarise in a table: worm, mode of infection, symptoms, prevention.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ascaris is a long, unsegmented, creamy roundworm; Taenia is a flat, ribbon-like segmented worm with a scolex; hookworm is small with a curved front end; guinea worm emerges through a skin blister.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A female Ascaris lays about 200,000 eggs per day: in one week 200,000 x 7 = 1,400,000 eggs pass in the stool, showing why proper faeces disposal is vital. Taenia solium can grow to 2-7 m; a 3 m worm with segments about 5 mm long would have roughly 3,000 / 5 = 600 segments.
precautions: Draw from the specimen, not memory
sourcesOfError: Preserved specimens shrink and lose colour
commonMistakes: Confusing the intermediate host of Taenia solium (pig) with the definitive host (human)
examTips: Write life cycles as clear arrows with stage names
Give one specific prevention for each stage

practicals.title: Reading health product labels and checking expiry dates
practicals.aim: To examine labels of drugs, foods and cosmetics for NAFDAC registration numbers, manufacturing and expiry dates, ingredients and storage instructions, and detect signs of fake or expired products.
apparatus: Phone (for NAFDAC Mas/scratch-code verification where available)
materials: Empty packets and containers of paracetamol, ORS, multivitamin syrup, tinned tomato, body cream, bottled water
safety: Use empty or sealed containers only; do not open or taste medicines
procedure: Examine each label and record: product name, manufacturer, NAFDAC registration number, batch number, manufacturing date, expiry date, ingredients, dosage, storage.
Check for signs of fakes: spelling errors, poor printing, missing NAFDAC number, broken seals, unusual price.
Calculate the shelf life and whether each product is still safe on the date of the practical.
Read the storage instructions (e.g. "store below 25 degrees C, away from sunlight").
Discuss the agencies protecting consumers: NAFDAC, Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON), Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC).
Record results in a table and state which products should not be bought or used.
practicals.expectedObservations: Genuine products have clear printing, a NAFDAC number, batch number and readable dates; some samples may be expired or lack details.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A syrup manufactured in March 2025 with an 18-month shelf life expires in September 2026 (March 2025 + 18 months). On a practical date of 22 October 2026 it has been expired for about 1 month and must not be used. Of 12 products examined, 2 were expired: 2 / 12 x 100 = 16.7%.
precautions: Read dates carefully - formats differ (DD/MM/YY, MM/YYYY)
commonMistakes: Confusing manufacturing date with expiry date
Assuming a high price means the product is genuine
examTips: Name the agency and its role
List label features of a genuine product

checkQuestions.explanation: NAFDAC regulates food, drugs and cosmetics.

practicals.title: Inspection of housing for health standards
practicals.aim: To inspect a room or house for siting, ventilation, lighting, sanitation and overcrowding against health criteria.
safety: Work in groups with permission of occupants; respect privacy
Do not enter unsafe or collapsing structures
procedure: Measure the floor length and width of a room and calculate the floor area.
Measure all window openings and calculate the total window area.
Compare window area with floor area (a common guide is at least 10% for ventilation/lighting).
Count occupants and calculate floor space per person.
Check toilet, bathroom, kitchen, drainage, refuse disposal, water source and distance of pit latrine from wells (at least 30 m).
Write a report with recommendations.
practicals.expectedObservations: Some rooms have too few windows or are overcrowded; poor drainage and close latrines threaten health.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Room 4 m x 3.5 m = 14 m2. Minimum window area at 10% = 1.4 m2. Two windows of 1.0 m x 0.6 m = 2 x 0.6 = 1.2 m2, which is below 1.4 m2 - ventilation is inadequate. If 4 people sleep there, space per person = 14 / 4 = 3.5 m2.
precautions: Record all openings, including doors used for ventilation separately
examTips: Show area calculations with units
Link poor housing to diseases (TB, CSM, cholera)

practicals.title: Visit to a primary health centre or school clinic
practicals.aim: To observe the services of a primary health care centre (immunisation, antenatal care, health education, records) and analyse immunisation coverage data.
safety: Follow staff instructions; do not touch equipment or patients
Wash hands on arrival and departure; wear a mask if advised
procedure: Obtain permission and prepare questions in advance.
Observe services offered: immunisation, antenatal and postnatal clinics, family planning, treatment of common illnesses, health talks.
Note how records (immunisation cards, registers) are kept.
Obtain anonymised summary figures (e.g. children due for immunisation and those fully immunised).
Calculate coverage and compare with the national target.
Write a report with recommendations.
practicals.expectedObservations: The centre provides preventive and curative services; immunisation schedules and health records are kept; coverage may fall short of targets.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Of 240 children aged 12-23 months registered, 180 were fully immunised: coverage = 180 / 240 x 100 = 75%. To reach a 90% target, 0.9 x 240 = 216 children must be fully immunised - 36 more.
precautions: Ask questions politely and record answers accurately
commonMistakes: Not linking findings to primary health care components
examTips: Name components of PHC (immunisation, MCH, health education, safe water, essential drugs)
Show coverage calculations
